t: Monte Albán was founded on a mountain in the no-man's-land between three rival valley societies, and its early pottery suggests settlers came from San José Mogote.
The Zapotec developed a logosyllabic writing system thought to be one of the first in Mesoamerica; it remains undeciphered.
The Zapotec called themselves by a variant of Be'ena'a, the Cloud People, from their elite's belief that they descended from beings who lived among the clouds.
dyk: Building J at Monte Albán, shaped like an arrowhead, carries more than 40 carved stones that archaeologists read as the provinces the Zapotec controlled; upside-down heads on them are believed to stand for rulers killed in conquest.
ev: In the Rosario phase three rival societies divide the valleys of Oaxaca, and at its end San José Mogote loses most of its population
The state formed at Monte Albán begins to expand beyond the valley
Zapotec expansion peaks in the Monte Alban 2 phase, by conquest and by colonisation
Monte Albán ceases to be the largest city in the southern Mexican highlands
The last battle between the Aztecs and the Zapotec is fought at Guiengola under the Aztec ruler Ahuizotl
Francisco de Orozco arrives in the Valley of Oaxaca, and the Zapotec soon submit to the rule of Hernán Cortés

f.homeland: The Central Valleys of Oaxaca in southern Mexico (Etla, Ocotlán and Mitla), about 200 km south of Mexico City; key sites Monte Albán, San José Mogote, Mitla, Lambityeco, Dainzú, Yagul, El Palmillo, Zaachila and Guiengola on the Isthmus of Tehuantepec
f.period: Rosario phase (700–500 BCE); Monte Alban 1 (late phase 400–100 BCE); Monte Alban 2 (c. 100 BCE – 200 CE), the peak of expansion; Monte Albán the largest city of the southern Mexican highlands until about 700 CE; Aztec conquest of the area in 1458; Spanish rule from 1521
f.known: Monte Albán and its monumental buildings, ball courts and tombs; one of the first writing systems of Mesoamerica; a calendar; building J, the "Conquest Slab"; finely worked gold jewellery; the ruins of Mitla; canal irrigation
f.sources: Excavations at Monte Albán, begun by Alfonso Caso in the 1930s; the work of Joyce Marcus and Kent V. Flannery; colonial-era sources on the gods, compiled by Michael Lind; legends written down after the Spanish conquest; finds by Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH)
